analysis.one_liner: Requires websites and internet providers to get your permission before collecting or selling your personal information.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 11 Senate sponsors, all Democrats, the bill got one committee hearing in October 2000 and never a vote; it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set the first federal rules for how companies collect and sell personal information online. Websites, internet providers, and advertisers would need your advance permission before gathering or sharing details like your name, address, email, or credit card number, and they would have to tell you when your data was leaked. It extended existing video-rental privacy law to books and music, gave the FTC enforcement power, let individuals and state attorneys general sue violators, and extended cable-style privacy rules to satellite TV customers. The bill never left the Senate Commerce Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Internet users and consumers generally. Anyone whose browsing, purchases, or account details were being gathered and sold would gain the right to notice, advance consent, access to their own files, and the ability to sue companies that violated the rules, with damages of $5,000 per violation and up to $50,000 for willful violations [S2][S3]. Renters and buyers of books and music would get the same confidentiality protection video renters already had [S2][S3]. Satellite TV subscribers would get the notice-and-consent protections cable subscribers already had [S2]. Workers would gain protection against being fired for reporting privacy violations [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Websites, online services, and internet providers could not collect or share personally identifiable information without clear notice and the user's advance, affirmative consent, and consent could only be changed by the user, surviving company mergers and policy changes [S2][S3].
Companies would have to let users see and correct their information, keep it secure, and notify users after any privacy breach [S2][S3].
The bill extended the existing criminal ban on disclosing video rental records to books and recorded music, so a person's reading and listening habits could not be sold [S2][S3].

Enforcement was real: FTC enforcement, a private right to sue for $5,000 per violation (up to $50,000 for willful violations), state attorney general lawsuits, and whistleblower protection for employees who report violations [S2][S3].

Satellite TV subscribers would get the same subscriber-privacy protections cable customers already had, and phone carriers would need express prior authorization before sharing customers' network usage data [S2][S3].
Personal information could no longer be treated as an asset sold off when a company went bankrupt [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial websites, internet and online service providers, advertisers, and data brokers would bear the cost of compliance: obtaining consent before collection, providing access and correction, securing data, and facing lawsuits with statutory damages for violations. Any business selling or reselling customer data as a revenue stream would lose that business [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Websites, ISPs, advertisers, and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts state laws inconsistent with it, which would override stricter state privacy rules, though it preserves state tort, common law, and fraud claims and any state private rights of action [S3].

For information that is not personally identifiable, the bill works on an opt-out basis: users are deemed to have consented unless they object, a weaker standard than the opt-in rule for personal data and one that leaves behavioral tracking mostly permissible if it stops short of identifying a person [S3].
Liability of $5,000 per violation and mandatory consent and security procedures would impose real compliance costs, falling hardest on small websites and startups [S3].

Companies could still collect and use information without consent to complete a transaction the user asked for and to protect their own systems, a carve-out broad enough for routine commercial data use [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protections were stronger than anything Congress has since enacted at the federal level, with consent required up front and individuals able to sue. The main honest costs are compliance burdens on small operators and liability exposure, and the opt-out loophole for non-identifying data would have left much behavioral tracking legal even as written. On balance the bill's benefits to consumers clearly outweighed those costs, which is why its quiet death matters: two decades later, Congress has still not passed a general online privacy law of this scope.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2000 with 10 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which held one hearing in October 2000 but never voted on it, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Sen. Ernest Hollings introduced the Consumer Privacy Protection Act on May 23, 2000, joined by 10 Democratic cosponsors [S4][S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
The committee held hearings on the bill on October 3, 2000, printed as S.Hrg. 106-1147 [S5].
No markup, committee vote, floor action, or House companion action followed, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 with the bill still in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online advertisers, data brokers, and website operators were better off: without a law, they kept the unrestricted ability to collect, use, and sell user data that the bill would have ended, while consumers were left with no general federal online privacy right at all.

for.name: Sen. Ernest Hollings
for.role: U.S. Senator from South Carolina (lead sponsor)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; the bill was referred to the Commerce Committee, on which he served.

for.name: 10 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction: Rockefeller, Bryan, Breaux, Inouye, Feingold, Edwards, Kerrey, Cleland, Durbin, and Byrd.

against.name: Sen. John McCain
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: The committee under his chairmanship held one hearing but never scheduled a markup or committee vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Internet, advertising, and direct-marketing industries
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal online privacy legislation and pressed Congress to let industry self-regulation stand, the policy approach the bill's own findings said had produced no enforceable consumer protection.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 Senate sponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the Republican-run Commerce Committee held a hearing but never brought the bill to a vote before the Congress ended.

industries.note: Their business model depends on collecting, combining, and selling information about what people do online, often without meaningful notice. Opt-in consent plus a private right to sue would have cut off the resale of personal data, which is why the bill's failure left this industry free to grow unregulated [S3].

industries.industry: Commercial websites, ISPs, and online service providers
industries.note: They would have faced consent, access, security, and breach-notification duties plus statutory damages, a real cost. The bill's own findings argued trust would help e-commerce, but the industry's position at the time was that self-regulation should replace legislation [S2][S3].

The bill extended video-rental privacy law to their customer records, making retailers liable for wrongful disclosure of what a customer bought or rented, including their reading and listening choices [S3].
They would gain the same subscriber-privacy rules cable operators already followed, adding obligations but putting them on equal footing with cable in a convercing market [S2][S3].
